title: Tranquillity by design: Architectural and landscape interventions to improve the soundscape quality in urban areas exposed to aircraft noise
central_proposition: Applying a combination of urban and architectural design strategies can improve the soundscape quality of areas exposed to aircraft noise and/or lead to a reduction of the sound exposure level.

concept_definitions.name: Soundscape
concept_definitions.definition: An ‘acoustic environment as perceived or experienced and/or understood by a person or people, in context’.

concept_definitions.name: Quiet building side
concept_definitions.definition: A facade without direct exposure to a noise source (nLOS), where the LAeq is <45dB(A), or where the relative difference with the exposed facade (LAeq) is >10dB(A).

concept_definitions.name: Noise annoyance
concept_definitions.definition: A ‘socio-technical’ issue which cannot be explained and solved by changing the sound exposure level alone.

concept_definitions.name: Coping
concept_definitions.definition: An individual’s ability to adjust the local environment to exogenous factors and to deal with a situation.

concept_definitions.name: Disturbance
concept_definitions.definition: Only triggers annoyance when people feel they cannot control mitigating the noise and/or lack the ability to cope with it.

concept_definitions.name: Refraction
concept_definitions.definition: The speed of sound gradient changes, and thus the direction of the vector normal to the wave front.

concept_definitions.name: Soundscape pleasantness
concept_definitions.definition: Relates to the roughness, sharpness and tonality of a sound.

concept_definitions.name: Soundscape eventfulness
concept_definitions.definition: Represents the descriptions of liveliness and ambiance (e.g. the level of human sounds).

argument_structure: The dissertation first establishes the problem of aircraft noise annoyance and the limitations of current abatement strategies, particularly the neglect of urban design and non-acoustic factors. It then reviews existing literature on sound propagation in urban areas, sound perception, and noise prediction models, highlighting research gaps. Four empirical studies are then presented: in-situ measurements to quantify noise reduction by buildings; development and validation of a numerical model to predict aircraft noise propagation around buildings, including atmospheric effects; a parametric study using the validated model to assess the impact of architectural design variables on noise reduction; and a virtual reality experiment to investigate the perceptual effects of natural features (water, vegetation) on soundscape quality and aircraft noise saliency. Finally, the results of these studies are synthesized to answer the main research question and provide recommendations for design practice and future research.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Architectural and urban design elements (building height, form, cladding, street canyon dimensions, ground materials) physically alter the propagation paths of aircraft noise through reflection, absorption, diffraction, and scattering, thereby reducing sound pressure levels at specific receiver locations, especially on shielded facades and at greater distances from flight paths. Atmospheric refraction also modulates these propagation paths. Concurrently, natural features (visible vegetation, moving water sounds) influence human perception of the acoustic environment by non-energetic masking, informational masking/distraction, visual attentional distortion, and by fostering congruence with expectations for pleasant environments, contributing to a sense of control and restoration, which in turn reduces annoyance.

findings.antecedent: Buildings (at substantial horizontal distance from flight path)
findings.consequent: Aircraft noise levels (LAmax and LAeq) near shielded facades
findings.mechanism: Buildings physically block, diffract, and scatter sound waves, creating a 'quiet' side. The effectiveness depends on distance from source, flight altitude, and building shape.
findings.source: 9.1 Final conclusions and discussion, Answer to Question 1
findings.quote: Buildings can reduce aircraft noise substantially, with LAmax and LAeq levels above 10dB(A) lower near shielded facades
findings.empirical_support_cited: Results from in-situ measurements (Chapter 5) show LAmax and LAeq levels >10dB(A) lower near shielded facades.

findings.antecedent: Atmospheric effects (refraction) in urban acoustic models
findings.consequent: Accuracy of aircraft noise prediction around buildings
findings.mechanism: Atmospheric refraction alters sound propagation paths, and neglecting it can lead to overestimation of noise reduction by models, especially at lower slant angles or substantial aircraft altitudes.
findings.source: 9.1 Final conclusions and discussion, Answer to Question 2
findings.quote: atmospheric effects can be omitted if the slant angle between a building and the position of an aircraft is greater than 15 degrees.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Numerical experiments (Chapter 6) comparing different refraction models to measurements.

findings.antecedent: Building geometry (loggias, overhanging roofs, height) and surface cladding (green walls) in urban areas (at substantial horizontal distance from flight path)
findings.consequent: Reduction of aircraft noise around buildings
findings.mechanism: Increased building height and protrusions extend the path length for sound waves and increase diffraction. Green walls add absorption. These elements physically block, diffract, absorb, and scatter sound waves, particularly for specific frequencies.
findings.source: 9.1 Final conclusions and discussion, Answer to Question 3
findings.quote: building geometry (loggias and overhanging roofs), building height, the width between facades and the surface cladding have a significant influence
findings.empirical_support_cited: Numerical simulations (Chapter 7) show added noise reduction well above 10dB for specific frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Presence of natural features (visible vegetation, moving water) in urban areas exposed to aircraft noise
findings.mechanism: Natural features contribute to non-energetic masking, visual attentional distortion, and congruence between visual and auditory expectations, leading to a more positive perception of the acoustic environment and reducing annoyance.
findings.source: 9.1 Final conclusions and discussion, Answer to Question 4
findings.quote: The presence of natural features, either visually, auditory or a combination of both, improve the soundscape quality of urban areas exposed to aircraft noise.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Virtual reality experiment (Chapter 8) shows significant improvement in soundscape quality.

findings.antecedent: Moving water (water jets) in urban areas exposed to aircraft noise
findings.consequent: Saliency and dominancy of aircraft flyovers
findings.mechanism: Moving water acts as an auditory masker, confusing the auditory signal of unwanted sounds and shifting attention away from aircraft noise (informational masking).
findings.source: 9.1 Final conclusions and discussion, Discussion of Question 4
findings.quote: Moving water clearly reduced the saliency of air and road traffic noise. This changes the constellation of fore- and background sounds and the audibility of the most dominant sound source.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Virtual reality experiment (Chapter 8) shows moving water was perceived as more dominant than aircraft noise, changing the order of fore- and background sounds.

findings.antecedent: Combination of visible vegetation and moving water
findings.mechanism: The combined effect of visual and auditory natural features is cumulative, enhancing the positive perceptual experience beyond individual interventions.
findings.quote: Compared to scenarios featuring either water features or vegetation, mean ratings for scenarios combining both interventions were higher for both soundscape pleasantness and eventfulness
findings.empirical_support_cited: Virtual reality experiment (Chapter 8) shows higher mean ratings for scenarios combining both interventions.

findings.consequent: Difference between exposed and shielded facades in sound levels
findings.mechanism: When streets are orthogonal to the flight path, both sides of the street canyon are exposed to direct sound waves at some point, blurring the distinction between exposed and shielded facades.
findings.quote: If the direction of the streets is orthogonal to the flight path, the differences between formerly exposed and shielded positions in a canyon will vanish.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Numerical simulations (Chapter 7) show that for configurations rotated by 90°, the difference between shielded and exposed sides seemingly disappears or reverses.

findings.antecedent: Narrow street canyons with tall buildings (close to flight path)
findings.mechanism: Reflected sound waves can become trapped within narrow canyons, leading to resonance and amplification of sound levels, especially for lower frequencies where absorption is less effective.
findings.source: 9.1 Final conclusions and discussion, Discussion of Question 3
findings.quote: For locations relatively close the flight path, the results show that a narrow canyon can reduce, or in the worst case negate, noise-abating effects due to trapped reflections between the buildings.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Numerical simulations (Chapter 7) show that narrow canyons can reduce, or in the worst case negate, noise-abating effects due to trapped reflections.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: To what extent do buildings reduce aircraft noise in areas that are not directly underneath flight paths as the distance between the aircraft and a receiver increases?
To what extent can urban acoustic models predict aircraft noise around buildings with an acceptable accuracy without considering atmospheric effects?
To what extent can the design of buildings and street canyons improve the reduction of aircraft noise locally within areas that are not directly underneath flight paths?
To what extent can visual and auditory natural features improve the soundscape quality of urban areas exposed to aircraft noise?
bridge_warrants: The paper explicitly links acoustic measurements (dB levels) with psychological perception (annoyance, soundscape quality).
It bridges urban acoustic modeling with aircraft noise prediction by developing a hybrid method.
It connects architectural and urban design variables to both acoustic attenuation and perceptual improvement.
It applies soundscape theory (pleasantness, eventfulness, masking, restorativeness) to the specific context of aircraft noise.
It uses virtual reality as a tool to study multisensory perception in soundscapes.
methodological_critiques: Traditional aircraft noise prediction models (INM, doc.29) omit buildings and only consider ground reflections.
Urban acoustic models lack validated methods to simulate aircraft flyovers.
Dose-effect curves for annoyance vary over time and between airports, and only predict a small proportion of variance in annoyance ratings.
Literature on non-acoustic factors is mainly inductive, lacking supporting theory and appropriate statistical methods for feedback loops.
Aircraft auralization models omit surface reflections and edge diffractions.
Ray-tracing models can suffer from caustics and shadow zones, leading to unrealistic sound pressure predictions.
Simplified refraction models (e.g., linear gradient) can overestimate sound attenuation.
Numerical models may underestimate noise reduction by buildings for higher frequencies in some cases.
There is a lack of standardized questionnaires for soundscape research, especially when using virtual reality.
model_structure: The paper does not propose a single new formal model, but rather evaluates and integrates existing approaches (urban acoustic models, aircraft noise prediction models, soundscape perception frameworks) to create a 'design toolkit'. It tests a hybrid numerical method for aircraft noise propagation around buildings and explores a soundscape perception framework in VR.
limitations: The research often examined how existing theories and methods can be harnessed for a different sound source (airplanes), rather than developing entirely new theories.
The variety of studies limited the time that could be spent per theme or topic, making it not always possible to set up follow-up experiments or validate results by more detailed models.
The numerical model underestimates the noise reducing potential of buildings in some cases, especially for higher frequencies, and assumes shielding effects decay too fast.
The model omits interference between sound waves for lower frequencies in very specific cases.
The model omits smaller facade ornaments, ledges, window frames, and material variations of the building surface to limit computational overhead.
The ray-tracing character and settings of the model (e.g., maximum number of reflections) influence the results.
The model's binary effect of curved rays can lead to sudden jumps in sound level predictions.
The sample size for the perception study was small.
The metrics used to measure overall quality, visual quality, auditory quality, and auditory pleasantness in the VR study were not orthogonal and thereby independent.
Long-term data is needed to study sound levels around buildings for a wider variety of weather types and seasons.
More comprehensive data collection (full perimeter of a building) is needed to chart the sound field in between buildings.
Additional in-situ research is recommended to verify the sound reduction yielded by green walls, as the numerical model's predictions might be conservative.
Further research is needed to identify the possible influence of building geometry on the interference of low-frequency sound waves in bays or between buildings.
Validation of the numerical model with results from wind tunnel tests is recommended.
The VR study only focused on public areas (squares and streets), not more private outdoor environments like gardens.
Future research could compare the foliage density and coverage, or the perception of aircraft noise in combination with different fountain designs.
The impact of source visibility on the perception of aircraft noise, in relation to the effectiveness of natural features, should be studied.
The response to aircraft noise in combination with natural features needs to be studied for more than two sound levels to improve estimations for equivalent noise reduction.

paper_metadata.title: Tranquillity by design : architectural and landscape interventions to improve the soundscape quality in urban areas exposed to aircraft noise

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Architectural and landscape interventions can be designed to positively influence the perception of sound environments, moving beyond mere noise reduction to enhance overall soundscape quality and tranquillity.

mechanism_chain.description: Buildings act as physical barriers, obstructing the direct line of sight and sound propagation path from aircraft, leading to a reduction in noise levels at facades located in the acoustic shadow.
